title: Fit a shifter fork over its spring-loaded ball: hold the ball flush with a screwdriver as the fork's bore runs over it
instruction: Fit the shifter fork onto the shifter rod over the indexing ball and leave it in neutral, then put the screwdriver back in its holder and let go.
context: A step in assembling or rebuilding a lawn-tractor transaxle, work of team assemblers (O*NET 51-2092.00, who assemble products from parts on lines and benches) and of outdoor power equipment mechanics (O*NET 49-3053.00, who repair and overhaul such drive units). The maker's technician's handbook: slide the shifter fork onto the rod until it comes to the hole with the indexing ball and spring; press the ball into the hole with a flat screwdriver and move the fork completely onto the rod; then move it to neutral, whose groove is seen through the hole in the fork. The skill is a hand-over between two hands: one holds the sprung ball flush with the screwdriver's blade while the other runs the fork's bore up to the blade, and the blade lifts away just as the bore takes the ball over.
setup: Two YAM arms at the near edge of a table; positions are (x forward from the arm bases, y left) in cm, heights above the table. An open transaxle case half of cast aluminium (19 x 22 cm, walls 5 cm high, open at its -y end) stands at x 19.5 to 38.5, y -10.5 to 11.5. The shifter rod, 9.5 mm steel, runs along y at x 30, 3 cm up, through bosses in an inner web and the far end wall; its free end comes out of the case's open end to y -12. A 6.35 mm indexing ball stands half out of a cross hole on top of the rod at y -3, on a spring; a stop holds it there (on the real rod nothing does, and an uncovered ball springs out). Beside the rod run a lay shaft carrying the shift collar and a gear, and a second shaft with another gear (drawn only). The shifter fork (150 g) lies on a rest in a tray at (25.5, -20): its hub, 20 mm long with an 11.2 mm bore, three detent grooves inside 7 mm apart (the middle one neutral) and a sight hole through its top over the neutral groove; an arm toward -x, 12 mm thick; a two-tined yoke at the arm's end, which fits round the shift collar at neutral. A cast rib under the arm's path keeps the fitted fork from swinging round the rod. A stubby flat screwdriver (105 mm, 6 mm blade, 30 mm handle) stands blade-down in a holder at (20, 15). The arms start at their ready pose.
scoring: Checked by looking through the fork's sight hole, a photo and a video of the trial, as an assembler checks. 1.0: the fork on the rod (its hub's axis within 8 degrees of the rod's) with the ball risen into the neutral groove (its middle within 0.5 mm of the groove's centre), the ball never lost, the fork never dropped, the screwdriver back upright in its holder and every fingertip 4 cm or more from the hub's middle, held 1 s. 0.5: the fork over the ball, without the 1.0 result. 0.25: the fork on the rod up to the ball. 0: the ball lost at any time (pressed in, then let up with neither the blade nor the fork over it: in the shop it springs out), the fork dropped (its middle below 12 mm above the table after it was lifted), or the fork not on the rod.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at 240 Hz on GPU. The handbook leaves the ball's seat open: built with ball and spring in the rod's cross hole and the three detent grooves inside the fork's bore, the neutral one under the sight hole. The ball is on a preloaded prismatic spring (2 N out, 4 N flush, guessed), up-weighted to 3 g. The bore's entry edge is square, so an unpressed ball stops the fork. The bore is 11.2 mm on the 9.5 mm rod, looser than the real fit, for a 20-sided collider.
